summary: For ages 8–9, teach the commutative, associative and distributive properties as calculation STRATEGIES (not named laws to memorise) that leave a total invariant. Prove each property visibly in an array/area model first, then use it to make a hard calculation easy. Centre the distributive split (8×7 = 8×5 + 8×2) as the highest-value strategy and the direct bridge to the area model and formal written multiplication. Explicitly contrast × (commutative/associative) with ÷ and − (neither), and prioritise strategy choice — which property is most efficient for a given calculation.
misconceptions: Applying the distributive split incorrectly — e.g. 8×7 = 8×5 + 2 (forgetting to multiply the second part) or splitting the wrong factor.
Treating the properties as names to memorise rather than strategies to use, so they aren't deployed in calculation.
Not seeing that the area model IS the distributive law, so written multiplication later feels disconnected.
Thinking reordering changes the answer, or conversely that any reordering is always allowed.

activities.title: Property playground: rotate, split, regroup on one array
steps: On an array/area canvas, meet an 'ugly' fact like 8×7. Drag a divider through the 7 to carve the array into 8×5 and 8×2; watch the two sub-rectangles light up as 40 and 16 and combine to 56.
Rotate the same array 90° and confirm the total does not change (8×7 = 7×8) — commutativity as 'same array, two orientations, same total'.
For three factors (2×3×5), toggle or drag the bracket between (2×3)×5 and 2×(3×5), and confirm the total holds — associativity as regrouping into an easier pair (6×5 or 2×15).

Switch to a division mode: swap the two numbers in a ÷ calculation (e.g. 32÷8 = 4 becomes 8÷32, which is less than 1) and see that the answer changes, then say in your own words why division is not commutative (32÷8 is not 8÷32).
Choose your own split for a new ugly fact (e.g. 8×9 = 8×5 + 8×4) and check the partial products add to the whole (40 + 32 = 72).
activities.insight: In multiplication, reordering, regrouping and splitting change how a calculation is written without changing its total; a hard multiplication fact can be cut into two friendly facts and reassembled. This 'cut-the-hard-one-into-two-easy-ones' move is the distributive property, and it is the same move that formal written multiplication later makes compact. Division and subtraction are not commutative or associative, so swapping or regrouping their numbers can change the answer.

activities.title: Split-area anchor for the distributive fact
steps: Study an area rectangle for 8×7 that is pre-split into 8×5 and 8×2.
Reveal the labels: left part '8×5 = 40', right part '8×2 = 16', whole '= 56'.
Answer the prompt 'Why does splitting the 7 into 5 and 2 not change the total?' before moving on.
activities.insight: The distributive split keeps the whole fixed because the two sub-rectangles together are exactly the original rectangle; 8×7 and 8×5 + 8×2 name the same quantity.

activities.title: Consolidate and sort: valid forms and the division trap
steps: Choose which expression equals 6×4, with 4×6 correct and 6÷4 and 4÷6 offered as tempting wrong choices.
Sort statements into 'always true' versus 'not true for division', e.g. is 32÷8 = 8÷32? Is (24÷4)÷2 = 24÷(4÷2)?
activities.insight: Property use can be checked and the overgeneralisation to division can be caught: reordering and regrouping hold for × but not for ÷.

activities.title: The lazy mathematician: justify the easiest strategy
steps: Talk with a 'lazy mathematician' character who always wants the easiest split or reorder for a given calculation.
When the character proposes a move (e.g. regroup 2×3×5 to 6×5, or split 7×6 into 5×6 + 2×6), explain why it gives the same answer.
Decide together which property is most efficient for different calculations and say why.
Catch the character out when it tries to 'reorder' a division or subtraction.
activities.insight: Choosing the most efficient property and justifying it out loud is part of fluent calculation; not every operation permits reordering.

checkQuestion: I know that 8 × 5 = 40. Without working out 8 × 7 the long way, can you use what you already know to figure it out? Tell me what you did and why it works.
checkAnswer: 8 × 7 = 56. A child reasoning correctly splits the 7: 8 × 7 is 8 × 5 plus 8 × 2, so 40 + 16 = 56 — because seven groups of eight is the same as five groups of eight and two more groups of eight (distributive property). Any valid split (8×7 = 8×6+8, or double 8×3.5 is not expected here) counts if the REASON is about decomposing one factor into parts that are added.
